lead: A new business location with employees (a shop, a branch, an office) opens in the US.

stem_fewer: Fewer than {t}% of new locations like it are still open a year later.
source_name: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Business Employment Dynamics
evidence: Table 7, survival rates since birth after one year: March 1995 453,105 4,135,330 79.6 79.6 9.1 (opened in the year to March 1994) | 2001 cohort: 75.7 | March 2007 560,076 3,547,086 78.3 78.3 6.3 (2006 cohort) | Chart 3, started 2014: 79.9
fact: BLS follows every new private-sector business location. A year after opening, between 75.7% and 79.9% were still open in the cohorts it reports (79.6% of those that opened in the year to March 1994, 78.3% of those in the year to March 2006).
why: Most new businesses survive their first year, and the failures people remember are the minority. Start from how often cases like this one survive, then adjust for what you know about this one.

why: Big names feel permanent, but the list turns over quickly: most of one generation's giants have shrunk, merged or vanished a generation later.

lead: Someone buys a single US common stock and holds it for its whole life.

fact: Hendrik Bessembinder's study of the CRSP records finds that 58% of US common stocks earned less over their whole lives than one-month Treasury bills.
why: The index looks good because a few stocks do spectacularly well; the typical stock does not. Betting on one stock is betting against the odds, whatever the story.

lead: Look at the US stock market as a whole since 1926 and ask where its gains over Treasury bills came from.

fact: In Hendrik Bessembinder's study, the entire gain of the US stock market since 1926 is attributable to the best-performing 4% of listed stocks.
why: A handful of giant winners produce the market's returns. Own only a few stocks and you will probably miss them, while a broad index owns them all.

fact: S&P's SPIVA scorecard (data to 31 December 2025): 85.59% of all active large-cap US funds underperformed the S&P 500 over ten years.

fact: SPIVA, year-end 2025: 79% of active large-cap US funds (78.78%) underperformed the S&P 500 in 2025, worse than the 65% of 2024.
why: A single year is a noisy test: 65% of managers lagged the index in 2024 and 79% in 2025. Long records tell you more than one good or bad year.

lead: A US adult is asked, in a Federal Reserve survey in October 2025, whether they could pay a surprise $400 expense with cash or its equivalent.

why: Most households can absorb a small shock, but a large minority cannot. When you judge how someone will cope with a surprise bill, remember how thin many cushions are.

lead: A city wins the right to host an Olympic Games and sets a budget.

stem_fewer: Fewer than {t}% of Games like it ended up costing more than budgeted, after inflation (the 19 Games from 1960 to 2016 with figures on record).

fact: In the Oxford Olympics Study every one of the 19 Games with data, from 1960 to 2016, ran over budget in real terms: 'cost overrun is found in all Games, without exception'.
why: Budgets for one-off mega-events are set before the hard problems appear. When a budget is the only estimate, the outside view says expect it to rise.

lead: A city wins the right to host an Olympic Games and sets a budget.

stem_fewer: On average, Games like it ended up costing less than {t}% over budget, after inflation.

fact: The Oxford Olympics Study puts the average overrun at 156% in real terms (median 90%) across the 19 Games from 1960 to 2016 with data: the average Games cost about two and a half times its budget.
why: Averages hide the shape: a few huge overruns drag the mean well above the median. For one project the median, 90%, is the better guide, and it is still large.

lead: A city wins the right to host an Olympic Games and sets a budget.

fact: In the Oxford Olympics Study, 9 of the 19 Games (47%) cost more than double their budget in real terms.
why: In nearly half the Games the final bill was more than twice the budget. When that happens close to one time in two, the official budget deserves little trust.

lead: A megaproject (a rail line, an airport, a tunnel, a dam, anything costing over a billion dollars) is approved with a budget.

fact: Bent Flyvbjerg's research on megaprojects (those costing over a billion dollars): 'Nine out of ten megaprojects have cost overruns.'
why: Over budget is the rule for giant projects, not the exception. Treat 'on budget' as the claim that needs evidence.

lead: A drug candidate starts its first trial in people (Phase I).

fact: Industry data on 12,728 drug programmes (BIO, Informa and QLS, 2011 to 2020): 7.9% of the programmes that entered Phase I were eventually approved.
why: The drug pipeline is a funnel with a narrow end: most candidates fail somewhere along the way, however good the early news. A promising first trial is a weak signal of an eventual medicine.

lead: A drug candidate is in its Phase I trial, the first test in people and mostly a check on safety.

fact: BIO's data for 2011 to 2020 (4,414 programmes): 52.0% of candidates moved from Phase I to Phase II.

lead: A drug candidate is in its Phase II trial, the first real test of whether it works.
stem_more: More than {t}% of candidates like it move on to Phase III.
stem_fewer: Fewer than {t}% of candidates like it move on to Phase III.

fact: BIO's data for 2011 to 2020 (4,933 programmes): 28.9% of candidates moved from Phase II to Phase III, the lowest rate of the four stages.
why: Phase II is where most drug hopes end: showing that a drug works is much harder than showing it is safe. Early promise is cheap; evidence of effect is not.

lead: A drug candidate is in its Phase III trial, the large final test before the company files for approval.
stem_more: More than {t}% of candidates like it go on to a filing for approval.

why: Once a drug has cleared its big trials and the filing is in, approval is the usual outcome. Judge a late-stage event differently from an early one.

lead: A cancer drug candidate starts its first trial in people (Phase I).
